Images.Description: Exploring Metabolic Reprogramming in Breast Adenocarcinoma

Header: Breast adenocarcinoma, most commonly presenting as invasive ductal carcinoma, arises from glandular epithelial cells and is marked by abnormal structures, cellular atypia, and metabolic reprogramming. Cancer cells enhance glycolysis, glutamine uptake, and lipid metabolism to support growth and resist therapy, making metabolic pathways promising targets for treatment.

Waypoints.Name: Tissue architecture
Waypoints.Description: Imaging Mass Cytometry using Pan-Cytokeratin, CD45, and αSMA markers reveals the complex architecture of breast adenocarcinoma, distinguishing malignant epithelial cells, immune infiltrates, and stromal fibroblasts. This spatial profiling highlights tumor heterogeneity, immune response, and stromal remodeling, offering insights into tumor progression and the tumor microenvironment.

Waypoints.Name: Glucose metabolism
Waypoints.Description: Breast adenocarcinoma displays metabolic reprogramming marked by elevated expression of GLUT-1 and LDHA, reflecting a reliance on aerobic glycolysis (the Warburg effect). GLUT-1 enhances glucose uptake, especially in hypoxic regions, while LDHA promotes lactate production to sustain glycolytic flux—both supporting tumor growth and correlating with aggressive clinical features. Their upregulation highlights potential therapeutic targets within cancer metabolism.

Waypoints.Name: mTOR signaling
Waypoints.Description: Elevated phosphorylation of mTORC1 downstream targets pS6 and p4EBP1 indicates increased protein synthesis and tumor cell proliferation, reflecting hyperactive mTOR signaling often driven by PI3K/Akt pathway alterations. This signaling activity is associated with tumor progression and therapy resistance, and can be suppressed by mTORC1 inhibitors like rapalogs to reduce tumor growth.

Waypoints.Name: Aerobic metabolism
Waypoints.Description: Markers such as ATP5A and citrate synthase reveal active mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS), indicating that many tumor cells retain aerobic respiration despite their reliance on glycolysis. This metabolic flexibility supports tumor growth and survival under varying conditions, including hypoxia and dormancy, highlighting the role of OXPHOS in cancer adaptation and progression.

Waypoints.Name: Immune and stromal cell activity
Waypoints.Description: Immune and stromal markers—CD8, CD4, CD14, and FAP—highlight a complex tumor microenvironment shaped by cytotoxic and helper T cells, monocyte-derived macrophages, and cancer-associated fibroblasts. This interplay of immune activation, regulation, and stromal remodeling influences tumor progression, immune evasion, and therapeutic response.
